column5: Hearing, fear, obedience, and well-being
column6: After Israel hears God’s voice at Horeb, YHWH wishes they would keep a heart to fear him and his commands always, so it would go well with them and their children; this directly joins heard instruction, reverent fear, and benefit.

column5: The God-fearer is taught the way
column6: The psalm asks who fears YHWH and answers that God will instruct that person in the way to choose; it reverses the commentary’s order in a useful way, making fear the disposition that receives instruction.

column5: Casting instruction behind oneself
column6: In God’s indictment of people who recite his statutes, the wicked are said to hate discipline and cast God’s words behind them; this makes rejection of instruction a deliberate act, close to the bedbaht’s avoidance.

column5: Refusal followed by one’s own counsel
column6: After Israel would not listen to God’s voice, the psalm says he gave them over to their stubborn hearts to walk in their own counsel; this connects refusal of a divine reminder with self-directed wandering.

column5: The good outcome of listening
column6: God says that if Israel would listen and walk in his ways, he would quickly subdue its enemies; the verse gives a concrete benefit that refusal has forfeited.

column5: The flock summoned to hear God’s voice
column6: The psalm calls Israel the people of God’s pasture and the sheep of his hand, then says “today, if you hear his voice”; it frames reception of divine speech as the present duty of the addressed community.

column5: Do not harden the heart when hearing
column6: The psalm warns its hearers not to harden their hearts as at Meribah; it makes the inner refusal that counters a receptive, trembling hearer explicit.

column5: Fear expressed by hearing and serving
column6: Samuel tells Israel that if they fear YHWH, serve him, and listen to his voice rather than rebel, they and their king will fare well; it directly links fear to taking divine instruction.

column5: Refusal brings the Lord’s hand against them
column6: Samuel warns that if Israel will not listen to YHWH’s voice and rebels against his command, the Lord’s hand will be against them; this gives the non-hearing side its consequence.

column5: Obedience is better than sacrifice
column6: Samuel tells Saul that listening to YHWH’s voice is better than sacrifice; the rebuke makes heedful response itself the required offering, not a religious substitute for it.

column5: Rejecting the word brings rejection
column6: Samuel says Saul rejected YHWH’s word, so YHWH rejected him as king; this states the consequence of a ruler who hears the divine command but will not receive it.

column5: Instruction as a path of life
column6: Proverbs says the one who heeds instruction is on a path of life, while the one who rejects reproof leads others astray; it gives both the benefit of receiving counsel and the danger of refusing it.

column5: The son who hears versus the scoffer
column6: A wise son hears his father’s instruction, while a scoffer does not listen to rebuke; this is another precise contrast between a teachable recipient and one who avoids admonition.

column5: A stiff neck after repeated reproof
column6: The person often reproved who stiffens his neck will suddenly be broken beyond healing; this develops the fate of persistent refusal beyond the single act of avoiding a reminder.

column5: Willing obedience and good outcome
column6: Isaiah says that if the people are willing and obedient they will eat the good of the land; it specifies a benefit for taking the prophetic demand to heart.

column5: Refusal and rebellion bring destruction
column6: The paired warning says that if the people refuse and rebel, they will be devoured by the sword; it makes refusal of the same summons a concrete opposite outcome.

column5: Hearing without understanding in Isaiah’s commission
column6: Isaiah is told to tell the people to hear without understanding and see without perceiving; in its own setting this is a prophetic commission to an unreceptive audience, offering a stark counter-scene to the commentary’s hearer who takes admonition.

column5: A people unwilling to hear instruction
column6: Isaiah calls them rebellious children who will not hear the instruction of YHWH; this directly names refusal of the teaching the commentary calls a reminder.

column5: Demanding smooth words from the prophets
column6: The people tell seers not to see and prophets not to speak what is right, but to prophesy smooth things; this gives a specific way of avoiding correction by trying to control what the admonisher may say.

column5: Asking the Holy One to leave
column6: They demand that the prophet turn aside from the way and that Israel’s Holy One cease from before them; this sharpens the commentary’s image of keeping the reminder at a distance into rejection of its divine source.

column5: The God-fearer listens to the servant’s voice
column6: Isaiah asks who fears YHWH and obeys the voice of his servant, then tells that person to trust in YHWH while walking in darkness; this joins fear and listening while adding trust in a difficult circumstance.

column5: The wicked are urged to turn and receive pardon
column6: Isaiah tells the wicked to forsake their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon; this shows prophetic admonition offered for a hearer’s benefit, not only to announce judgment.

column5: Turn so wrongdoing will not become ruin
column6: Ezekiel urges Israel to repent and turn from its transgressions lest iniquity become its downfall; this makes the warning’s practical benefit explicit.

column5: Turn and live rather than die
column6: YHWH says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death and commands Israel to turn and live; this places a life-giving invitation beside the commentary’s contrast of the one who receives counsel and the wretched one who avoids it.

column5: God calls the wicked to turn from death
column6: YHWH swears he takes no pleasure in the wicked person’s death but wants that person to turn and live, repeating “turn back”; it makes the offered warning’s life-preserving purpose unmistakable.

column5: Those who fear the Lord do not disobey his words
column6: Ben Sira says those who fear the Lord will not disobey his words and those who love him keep his ways; this directly links reverent fear with receiving and following instruction.

column5: Jerusalem is unwilling to be gathered
column6: Jesus says he often wanted to gather Jerusalem’s children as a hen gathers her brood, but they were unwilling; the image makes refusal of a protective summons concrete.

column5: The word held fast and made fruitful
column6: Jesus says good-soil hearers hold the word fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience; this specifies an enduring form of the beneficial reception described in the commentary.

column5: Take care how you hear
column6: Jesus warns his hearers to consider how they hear, since the one who has will receive more and the one who lacks will lose even what he thinks he has; this makes the consequences of response explicit.

column5: Blessing belongs to those who keep the word
column6: Jesus says blessed are those who hear God’s word and keep it; this pairs reception with obedience and the blessed outcome that contrasts with the commentary’s unhappy avoider.

column5: Hearing and believing lead from death to life
column6: Jesus says the one who hears his word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life; the verse links reception to a changed fate.

column5: Refusing to come for life
column6: Jesus tells his interlocutors that they are unwilling to come to him to have life; this is a direct instance of refusing the offered source of life.

column5: Rejected words become the judge
column6: Jesus says the one who rejects him and does not receive his words has a judge: the word he spoke will judge on the last day; it connects non-reception to the judgment that follows.

column5: Resisting the Spirit as the ancestors did
column6: Stephen accuses his hearers of always resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did; this gives rejection of divine speech a repeated communal history.

column5: Paul says his hearers thrust aside the word
column6: Paul and Barnabas say their audience judged itself unworthy of eternal life by thrusting aside God’s word, so they turn to the Gentiles; this concretely depicts a hearer’s active rejection of the announcement.

column5: Gentile hearers rejoice and believe
column6: The Gentiles rejoice when they hear Paul’s message and believe; this supplies the receptive counterpart in the same proclamation scene.

column5: Different responses to Paul’s explanation
column6: After Paul explains the kingdom of God and argues from Moses and the prophets, some are persuaded and others disbelieve; this is a clear scene of one teaching meeting divided responses.

column5: Pay closer attention lest hearers drift away
column6: Hebrews urges readers to pay closer attention to what they heard so they do not drift away from it; this makes avoidance a gradual slipping from an already heard warning.

column5: Neglecting salvation has no escape
column6: Hebrews asks how anyone can escape if they neglect such a great salvation; this adds the consequence of letting a saving announcement pass by.

column5: Do not refuse the one speaking
column6: Hebrews warns its readers not to refuse the one speaking from heaven and recalls that those who refused the earthly warning did not escape; it explicitly joins refusal of admonition with judgment.

column5: Receive the implanted word that can save
column6: James tells readers to put away wickedness and receive meekly the implanted word, which can save their souls; this makes admonition a saving gift that must be welcomed.

column5: Bringing a wanderer back from error
column6: James says whoever brings a person wandering from truth back saves that person from death and covers many sins; this gives the reminder a neighbor-directed, restorative action.

column5: Knowing God and hearing his messengers
column6: John says whoever knows God listens to the apostolic witnesses, while one not from God does not listen; this directly ties knowledge to receptivity, complementing the commentary’s discussion of knowledge and fear.

column5: Prophetic speech as judicial hardening
column6: Isaiah’s commission continues by telling him to make the people’s heart dull and ears heavy, lest they turn and be healed; unlike the commentary’s account of the wretched person avoiding a reminder, this passage portrays non-reception within a judgment commission.

column5: Discipline understood as a father’s instruction
column6: Moses tells Israel to know in its heart that YHWH disciplines it as a father disciplines a son; this offers a Jewish scriptural frame in which correction itself is instruction, though it does not describe the audience’s response to a spoken reminder.

column5: Sinai’s acceptance under threat and later reaffirmation
column6: The Talmud imagines the mountain held over Israel as a barrel, with acceptance of Torah demanded under threat of burial, then says Israel reaffirmed acceptance in Ahasuerus’s days; this complicates a simple equation of reception with inward reverent fear by distinguishing coerced and later willing acceptance.

column5: Isaiah’s hard-hearing prophecy applied to Paul’s audience
column6: Paul quotes Isaiah’s dull ears and closed eyes to explain why some hearers will not understand, turn, and be healed; this Christian continuation shows an interpretive tradition applying Isaiah’s account of failed reception to a new audience.

column5: Clement’s Jonah as a model of heeded warning
column6: Clement recalls that Jonah preached destruction to Nineveh and that the city repented and obtained pardon; this early Christian retelling reads the scriptural warning as a summons whose reception changes the announced outcome.
